extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, government legal advisors, military department officials, and scholars dealing with public property, military reservations, and national cemeteries
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal rules and standards governing rights, jurisdiction, duties, and procedures relating to military reservations, national cemeteries, and other public property (ownership, cession, trespass, interments, regulation). Designed to guide legal decision-making and administrative actions by federal and state authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander authority re: tidewaters and piscary rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Territory, in the absence of special regulation of the subject by Congress, no executive authority can lawfully restrict the common-law right of piscary of the inhabitants (including the taking of shellfish) in the tidewaters of the Territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commander of a reserved military post fronting upon navigable water of a Territory is not empowered to remove from such tidewaters the seines or traps of fishermen; though if the public interests require it he may forbid or restrict the use of the shore above high-water mark for the hauling of seines or landing of fish. (P. 15, 4-52, Mar., 1887.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expulsion and treatment of squatters on reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: Squatters and other trespassers may and should be expelled, by military force if necessary, from a military reservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If squatters have been suffered to own and occupy buildings on a reservation they should be allowed reasonable time to remove them; if not removed after due notice the military should remove them. Material abandoned by trespasser on vacating may be utilized by the commander for completing roads, walks, etc. (R. 49, 208, Julij, 1885; 60, 314, May, 1886; P. 64, 270, 303, Mar. & Apr., 1894.) Criminal proceedings under section 5388 R.S. may also be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War awards for squatters' improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where squatters have made considerable improvements and their value has been duly estimated by a board constituted by the department commander, an award by the Secretary of War, acquiesced in by the claimant, may be sued upon in the Court of Claims and will be accepted as conclusive in the absence of fraud or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award treated as conclusive unless evidence of fraud or mistake exists. (P. 17, 265, June, 1887; C. 12941, July 16, 1902; 16983, Oct. 8, 1904; 24196, Dec., 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting timber/grass and trespass offenses on reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: The cutting of timber on a military reservation is an offense against the United States (punishable under section 5388, R.S.); grass cut and removed as hay would be personal property and asportation would be larceny under March 3, 1875 acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons coming upon a military reservation to cut wood, grass, plow soil, or commit other trespass may be removed as intruders; the post commander may resort to military force if necessary and prevent trespassers from carrying off any property of the United States. (P. 64, 270, 303, Mar. & Apr., 1894; O. 3315, June, 1897; 16983, Oct. 8, 1904; 20531, 20544, 20818.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to remove injurious municipal intrusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The general principle of authority to remove trespassers, their structures and property from land of the United States embraced in a military reservation applies especially where the intrusion is for an injurious purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: preventing a municipality from laying a sewer intended to discharge into a U.S.-constructed main sewer. Municipal authorities should be given reasonable notice to remove property before resorting to military force and precautions should be taken to prevent connections to U.S. sewers. (P. 65, 6, May, 1894.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on contractors' commercial activities on reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor (e.g., a butcher under contract to supply the post) should not be permitted to sell goods on the reservation to citizens to the prejudice of local businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a contractor is not a post trader; Congress' specific provisions for post traders indicate legislation is necessary to authorize individuals to engage in trade at a military post. (P. 30, 475, Mar., 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for acquiring cemetery grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 4870-4872, R.S., constitute the only existing general law authorizing the purchase or acquisition of land as cemetery grounds for the interment of soldiers; earlier general provisions have ceased in force under section 5596.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation constrains acquisition authority to these sections. (P. 32, 261, May, 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of donated land for national cemetery
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to purchase property for a national cemetery includes authority to accept title by donation and to acquire rights of way thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, conditions attached to a proposed donation (e.g., that the U.S. build roads and substantial fence) may preclude acceptance. (C. 12242, Mar. 25, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eminent domain requisites for cemetery acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: To authorize acquisition by eminent domain of private land for a national cemetery under sections 4870 and 4871 R.S., there must be (1) an existing appropriation (in conformity with section 3736 R.S.) authorizing the acquisition; and (2) the private owner must be unwilling to give title or the Secretary of War unable to agree on price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both prerequisites are required before eminent domain may be exercised. (P. 32, 277, May, 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive appraisement by court for cemetery land
rubrics_metrics.description: The appraisement of land for a national cemetery as duly made by a United States court under sections 4871 and 4872 R.S. is conclusive upon the Secretary of War, who must pay the appraised value indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there has been fraud in the valuation or an excessive appraisement, the United States may properly move for a new appraisement. (R. 26, 617, June, 1868.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No obligation to establish cemetery for volunteer home burials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government is under no legal obligation to provide burial places for destitute soldiers at a volunteer home; section 4878's provision that certain soldiers 'may be buried in any national cemetery free of cost' does not require establishment of a national cemetery specifically for interments at such a home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute interpreted as permissive regarding locations. (P. 32, 277, May, 1889.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroad rights-of-way and national cemetery restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil sundry act of March 3, 1899 contains a provision that 'no railroad shall be permitted upon the right of way which may have been acquired by the United States to a national cemetery or to encroach upon any roads or walks constructed thereon and maintained by the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was intended to prevent occupation or encroachment of rights-of-way or roads to cemeteries but does not forbid granting permission to lay a railroad track across a Government roadway leading to a national cemetery. (C. 7466, Dec., 1899.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Traffic regulation on cemetery roadways without cession
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of any cession of jurisdiction over a cemetery roadway it is under the police jurisdiction of local authorities as to offenses committed thereon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no objection to posting notice that violations of local speed laws will be punished and to bringing violations to the attention of local authorities. (C. 26691, Sept. 2, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment rule applies only to easements, not fee simple
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory restriction in an appropriation that no part of funds be used for repairing any roadway within municipal limits should not be considered as an abandonment of a portion of the Government roadway where the title is in fee simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law regarding divestiture of title by abandonment applies where title is of an easement only, but has no application to a fee simple title. (C. 26103, Jan. 20, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and remedies concerning national cemetery superintendents
rubrics_metrics.description: Superintendents of national cemeteries are civilians (selected from persons honorably discharged) and are not part of the Army; they are not subject to the Articles of War or trial by court-martial; removal from office is the adequate remedy for serious misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory selection under section 4874 R.S.; relevant precedents cited. (R. 35, 34, Oct., 1873; 38, 381, Nov., 1876; 577, Apr., 1877.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest authority of cemetery superintendents limited
rubrics_metrics.description: By section 4881 R.S. the superintendent is authorized to arrest persons who injure gravestones, trees, shrubs, etc., within the cemetery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He could not legally arrest a person who fired a gun into or across the cemetery without causing any such specified injury; for such trespass he must have recourse to local authorities. (R. 32, 1425, Mar., 1872.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's rulemaking and enforcement authority in cemeteries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War may legally make rules for the use of roads within national cemeteries and for the rates of speed thereon, and any regulations so promulgated may be executed by the superintendent under the authority of section 4873 U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority to promulgate and enforce reasonable regulations within cemeteries. (C. 26691, May 10, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes entitled to interment in national cemeteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 4878 R.S. and the act of March 3, 1897, the following classes are entitled to interment in a national cemetery: (1) Officers/enlisted men who served in Regular or Volunteer Army or Navy during Civil War; (2) Officers/enlisted men who served during War with Spain; (3) Army nurses honorably discharged; (4) Officers/enlisted men who died while in military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where lots were assigned for burial of officers (e.g., Arlington) it was held permissible to permit interment of the remains of the wife or minor children of the officer to whom the lot was assigned. (C. 16508, June 22, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'Army nurses' entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of March 3, 1897 providing for interment of deceased Army nurses honorably discharged, the Secretary of War may place a liberal construction on the statute to permit assignment of a lot for persons whose duties were substantially that of superintendent of Army nurses even if not literally described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contract surgeon charged with superintending organization of Army nurses during Spanish War might be entitled. (C. 29060, Oct. 5, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'immediate vicinity' for burial appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the appropriation for burial of ex-Union soldiers, sailors, and marines 'who die in the District of Columbia, or in the immediate vicinity thereof,' the words 'immediate vicinity' should be interpreted reasonably to include towns near District boundaries whose inhabitants are employed in the District or regard it as center of business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is proper to include towns within a distance of 10 miles of the District line. (C. 16396, June 6, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of Revenue Marine Service members for cemetery interment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily the Revenue Cutter Service is not a part of the constitutional military or naval service and as such its members are not entitled to interment in a national cemetery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, when cooperating with the Navy under sections 1492 and 2757 R.S. they are to be considered part of the Navy during such service and entitled to burial in a national cemetery. (C. 19774, May 24, 1906; Nov. 25, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's authority under March 9, 1906 act for Confederate graves
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of March 9, 1906 authorized the Secretary of War to acquire possession or control of Confederate burial places, erect white marble headstones, build proper fencing, and care for burial grounds in all proper respects mentioned or not specifically mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary may do this without acquiring ownership of the land; appropriation covers necessary expenses, allows employing an architect and a stenographer; if graves cannot be identified, a suitable monument to the unidentified dead may be erected. (C. 19834, Apr. 1907; Nov., 1908; July, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority required for burials in designated cemetery sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War could not legally permit burials in specially set-apart cemetery sections (e.g., Confederate section at Arlington) in the absence of express statutory authority therefor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrangement to receive remains may be possible but burial uses are prescribed by statute; express authority is required. (C. £8774, July 29, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cession/purchase with state's consent conveys exclusive jurisdiction (constitutional clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction over territory in a State may be acquired by the United States, under clause 17 of section 8 of Article I of the Constitution, by the purchase of such territory with the consent of the State's legislature for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings; such consent invests the United States with exclusive jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution's grant is construed to mean exclusive jurisdiction (exclusive legislation). The consent must be a purchase with consent to bring the clause into play; exclusive jurisdiction usually means exclusive legislative authority over the place. (Discussion citing New Orleans v. U.S., U.S. v. Bevans, The Federalist No. 43.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'other needful buildings' should be construed narrowly
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'other needful buildings' in the constitutional clause should be read to mean buildings of the same character as those specified (i.e., intended for military or defensive purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more comprehensive construction has sometimes been given but is not justified; context and precedents indicate the term refers to similar territorial/military objects. (Citations: Story sec. 1224; In re Kelly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 355 R.S. consent requirement and effect on jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 355 R.S. prescribes that no public money shall be expended upon any site or land purchased by the United States for certain public buildings until the consent of the legislature of the State in which the land may be has been given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent of the State to a purchase given to satisfy section 355 would invest the United States with exclusive jurisdiction if the purchase is for a constitutional purpose; for other purposes consent may be accompanied by limitations and might only carry such jurisdiction as necessary for the purpose (possibly concurrent jurisdiction). (P. 355 discussion; C. 1953, Dec., 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Express cession by State as common method to acquire jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common way of acquiring jurisdiction is by the State's express cession to the United States; in such a case the State may make similar limitations, and this even if the place is used by the United States for a constitutional purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When jurisdiction is ceded the State may attach conditions or reservations (e.g., reservations of process-serving or taxation) which may limit scope; to bring case under the constitutional clause there must be a purchase with consent. (C. 1953, Dec., 1895.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership or reservation alone insufficient to create exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact of the United States being the owner of land situated within a State does not entitle the United States to exercise exclusive jurisdiction over the same or over offenses committed thereon, nor does mere reservation for military purposes confer such authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive jurisdiction over land within a State can only be vested in the United States by an act of cession of jurisdiction on the part of the State, or by the State's giving its consent to the purchase by the United States. (Citations: Ex parte Sloan, United States v. Stahl, etc.; P. 48–52.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cession required for exclusive jurisdiction over cemetery land within a State
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite statutory language (e.g., section 4872 R.S.) declaring jurisdiction 'exclusive' over land taken for a national cemetery by eminent domain, such exclusive jurisdiction cannot be legally vested in the United States if the land is within a State except by cession of the State legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An act of Congress is powerless to confer exclusive jurisdiction over land within a State absent cession. (K. 27, 661, May, 1869.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction ceases by operation of abandonment when reservation abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: When a military reservation is abandoned and turned over to Interior, there is no occasion for a statutory provision ceding back jurisdiction; jurisdiction ceases of itself with the use and occupation of the land for the purposes for which it was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some statutes have expressly limited grants, but such provisions are unnecessary; inference from constitutional clause that State relinquishes jurisdiction only for the term the particular status subsists. (P. 48, 475, Nov., 1890; O. 11668, Jan. 29, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-of-way grants do not oust exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of Congress granting a right of way across part of a military reservation does not operate to oust the exclusive jurisdiction previously ceded by the State to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such grants impose a duty on the military authorities not to interfere with the legitimate use of the right by the grantee (e.g., railroad). (P. 41, 457, July, 1890; O. 14323, Mar. 27, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified/conditional cessions are effective to the extent expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: A cession of jurisdiction by a State to the United States may be qualified or conditional, and concedes only so much as is specifically expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reservation of power to tax persons and corporations within a ceded military reservation was held constitutional and operative (C. 27365, Oct. 15, 1910). But conditions inconsistent with exclusive jurisdiction (e.g., retention of civil/criminal jurisdiction) may render the cession not of the exclusive character intended by the Constitution. (Various opinions: P. 59, 159, Apr.–May, 1893; O. 20606, Oct. 19, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservations to serve process may be compatible with exclusive jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A State reservation in ceding jurisdiction that the State reserves the right to execute process lawfully issued under its authority within the ceded sites may be regarded as reserving merely the right to serve process for acts done and crimes committed outside the same and thus the cession may still vest exclusive jurisdiction in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney General opinions and precedents indicate such narrow reservations do not defeat exclusive jurisdiction. (R. 142, 567, Apr. 3, 1880; 43, 234, Feb., 1880.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cessions 'concurrent with' State create doubt about exclusive status and appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a State statute consenting to purchase and ceding jurisdiction states that such jurisdiction shall be exercised 'concurrently with' the State, this qualification may be inconsistent with a grant of exclusive jurisdiction to the United States and may make it doubtful whether appropriations for erection of public buildings can be lawfully expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent jurisdiction language has been treated as more than the usual reservation to serve process and raises legal questions under section 355 R.S. (R. 43, Feb., 1880; P. 27, 132, Oct., 1888.)

rubrics_metrics.name: State may give prospective consent by general act
rubrics_metrics.description: A State may give its consent to purchase by the United States by a single general act, prospective in terms, covering all cases of future purchases by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such legislative acts have been recognized in Attorney General opinions and case law (e.g., act of Texas Apr. 4, 1871 discussed in AG Apr. 10, 1878).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader construction of 'needful' may vest exclusive jurisdiction (AG 1907)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Attorney General opinion dated July 3, 1907 held that the constitutional provision covers the purchase of land 'needful' for any reason to the discharge of any of the constitutional duties or the exercise of any of the constitutional powers of the United States, and that such purchase acquires exclusive jurisdiction over the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents a broader interpretation of 'other needful buildings' as related to discharge of constitutional duties. (26 Op. Atty. Gen., 289.)
